newsitem.title: USA: US aluminum premiums steady, 20 Stockpile bidders.
newsitem.headline: US aluminum premiums steady, 20 Stockpile bidders.

text.p: U.S. aluminum premiums remain steady with good demand supporting the market as 20 companies scrambled to buy aluminum from U.S. Stockpile, traders said.
Christopher Hill of Gerald Metals said physical aluminum was still well underpinned with LME recovering twice this year from dips this year, a sign of good consumer demand.
"There is an overall structural strength to the market," Hill said. "If anything the pressure is on the upside because there is still a lot of metal to be priced in the second half of this year."
The Midwest premium was quoted at 5.00 to 6.00 cents per lb for prompt metal, falling to about 4.5 cents in the second half of the year, and 4.25 cents on 1998 delivered metal.
Some 20 companies bid for 10,000 short tons of U.S. Stockpiled aluminum, offering premiums over LME cash in some cases compared to the discount to LME in the previous sale, traders said.

The bidders were VAW America, Reynolds Metals, Pechiney, Metal Exchange, Trans-World, Glencore, Alcoa, Alumax, F&S International, Easco, Gerald, Rochester Aluminum, Wise Metals, Hunter Douglas, Global Minerals and Metals, Barclays, Tenneco, Brown Industries, Mitsui, and Commercial Alloys.
Bid prices ranged from a low $1,240 a short ton from Alumax to a high of $1,511 from Reynolds. A Stockpile official said winners would be announced later today.
Broker GNI said the aluminum market was clearly in supply deficit but prices were held back by 1 million tonnes of idled capacity and rumors that some of this will be restarted.
Dealers repeated this week that Alcan's Sebree smelter on the Ohio river was a leading candidate for restarting capacity because it hired some employees recently.
Alcan spokesman Charles Belbin said the hiring at Sebree, where there are 60,000 tonnes of idled capacity, had nothing to do with restarting capacity.
"There has been no decision to restart capacity at this time. It depends on industry fundamentals," Belbin said.

GNI expected gradual restarts of idled capacity over the course of the next 18 months to two years. "At this rate the increase in supplies is likely to be more than offset by rising consumption as the momentum of recovery builds," GNI said.

Although LME stocks were still high at just under 800,000 tonnes, producer stocks were exceptionally low. Supply shortfalls will have to come from LME and much of this metal is tied up under financing deals, GNI said.
"This will tend to tighten the market structure, and could push aluminium into a backwardation," GNI added.
Both Gerald and GNI expected LME three months aluminum prices to rise this year.
Wednesday, LME three months cleared $1,640 per tonne in late London trading.

Gerald's Hill sees the market rising to $1,750 to $1,800 per tonne, with possible squeezes pushing the market higher at times. GNI saw LME three months close to $2,000 by year end, and a retest of this year's high of $1,701 was imminent.
